How to read this

  • Every screen is a proposal. None of it is built, and the Proposed pill in each header says so.
  • Click around inside each frame: the nav, the buttons, the arrows, and the pickers work. Nothing saves, and a reload puts everything back.
  • The numbers are Sam's made-up data, forecast with the app's real rule: a balance of $430.00 on Sep 26, two incomes, three expenses.

The stops

The screens in the order Sam would meet them. Each frame is the prototype itself, at the real viewport; the phone frames are small, so open one full screen when the words matter.

Overview

Sam's next 90 days, in order: the balance check-in, the answer in one sentence, the chart with a dot for every payment and the dip below zero shaded, three tiles, the balance history, and, as the last card, what is coming up.

AnswersErik 1Theo 7Theo 10.1Theo 11Erik: not just a spreadsheet

The answer and the chart

The sentence says what the chart shows: rent lands on Oct 1, before the first café shift, and Sam is $255 under until the second shift pays on Oct 10. On the chart every payment is a dot, green in and orange out, and the stretch below zero is shaded expense-orange. Switch to 30 or 180 days and the sentence follows.

Expense-orange is orange-600 (#ea580c) for dots, lines, fills, and badges, and orange-700 (#c2410c) for text on white, which keeps it readable at small sizes. Money in stays green. Buttons stay green too, because they are actions, not amounts.

Balance check-in and history

Saving a balance now says so, in the card and in a corner toast, and every balance is kept. Flip back to Sep 19 or Sep 12 and the chart redraws from that day, so the two of you can see how the forecast moved between check-ins.

AnswersErik 1Theo 10.1Theo 10.2

Coming up, month by month

Coming up is now the last card on the overview, not a page of its own: one month at a time, what comes in, what goes out, where the month ends, and every payment grouped by day. The arrows flip forward to December; September is as far back as it goes, because that is when Sam started.

AnswersTheo 9

Add an expense with the usual only

One amount, a rhythm, a next date, and a tag. The date field is styled like the rest of the form, with a calendar of its own instead of the browser's. A range is there for those who want it, folded away, and it starts equal to the usual.

AnswersErik 2Erik 3

Tags with a colour picker

Four presets, pay cheque, side hustle, bill, and groceries, plus one of Sam's own. Any colour: a swatch grid, a hue slider, or a hex value, styled like the rest of the app. Tags is back in the main nav; click a tag's name to open its own page.

AnswersErik 4Theo 4Theo 5Erik: only shades of green

A tag's page

Click a tag's name from the Tags screen and its own page opens: the tag's colour and name as the title, a one-line summary of what it adds up to, and its streams as cards, the same as on Income and Expenses.

AnswersTheo: keep tags, a tag shows its streams

Income and Expenses

The stream cards read as a sentence: the usual amount, the range if there is one, the rhythm, and the next date. Money out is expense-orange, money in stays green, and Add stays a green button.
